body.statement:
In the canonical full-observable experiment, suppose \(e_1\ne e_0\), \(p=1/2\), and \(\alpha+\beta<1\).  For every fixed \(a\) satisfying \(0<a\le2B\) and every integer \(n>4r+1\),
\[
 \frac{a^2(1-\alpha-\beta)}{\sqrt{2N_n}}
 \le s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}
 \le \rho_n(\alpha,\beta).
\]
Consequently, for fixed \(r,B,\varepsilon,\alpha,\beta\) with \(\alpha+\beta<1\) and \(p=1/2\),
\[
 s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}=\Theta(n^{-1/2}).
\]
The upper bound is attained by the unchanged sample-mean-centered test \(\phi_{n,\alpha}\), viewed as a Borel function of \(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\).  The lower bound ranges over every common Borel randomized test of the vector containing the observed graph, assignments, exposures, realized outcomes, and known propensity coordinates.
body.proof_tex:
We first prove the upper bound.  By the definition of the full observation, \(W_n\) is a Borel function of \(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\): each score is obtained from one realized outcome, the two exposure indicators, and the two strictly positive known propensity coordinates.  Hence the statistic \(\widehat\Omega_n^{12}\), and therefore \(\phi_{n,\alpha}\), is a common Borel function of \(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\).  The established size--separation theorem gives, uniformly over \(P\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\),
\[
 \mathbb E_P[\phi_{n,\alpha}]\le\alpha
 \quad\text{when }\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}=0,
 \qquad
 \mathbb E_P[1-\phi_{n,\alpha}]\le\beta
 \quad\text{when }\Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}\ge\rho_n(\alpha,\beta).
\]
The definition of \(s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}\) therefore yields
\[
 s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}\le\rho_n(\alpha,\beta). \tag{1}
\]

We prove the converse with an exact-local, causal-realizable, common-support submodel.  Fix \(a\in(0,2B]\) and put \(b=a/2\), so \(0<b\le B\).  Let the graph be the deterministic nearest-neighbor line, let \(U_i\) be iid \(\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]\) variables, take
\[
 E_i(d,G)=
 \begin{cases}
 e_1,&d_i=1,\\
 e_0,&d_i=0,
 \end{cases}
 \qquad
 C_i(d)=(d_i,d_{i+1})\in\mathcal C:=\{00,01,10,11\},
\]
and draw the two assignment waves conditionally independently with iid \(\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\) coordinates.  The innovation \(U_i\) is used to generate a random four-cell schedule
\(V_i=(V_{i,00},V_{i,01},V_{i,10},V_{i,11})\in\{-b,b\}^4\), independently over \(i\).  Define
\[
 \mathcal H_0
 =\{v\in\{-b,b\}^4:v_{10}+v_{11}-v_{00}-v_{01}=0\}.
\]
This set has six elements.  Let \(Q_0\) be uniform on \(\mathcal H_0\).  Put
\[
 v^+=(-b,-b,b,b),\qquad v^-=-v^+,
\]
in the coordinate order \((00,01,10,11)\), let \(Q_1\) assign probability \(1/2\) to each of \(v^+\) and \(v^-\), and, for \(0\le t<1\), set
\[
 Q_t=(1-t)Q_0+tQ_1. \tag{2}
\]
A finite quantile partition of \([0,1]\) realizes each \(Q_t\) as a measurable function of \(U_i\).  Under the resulting law \(P_t\), define the common no-carryover schedule by
\[
 Y_i(d;U,G)=V_{i,C_i(d)}. \tag{3}
\]
The line is shift equivariant and has edge range one.  The exposure and outcome rules in (3) are shift equivariant and depend only on \((U_i,d_i,d_{i+1})\), so they are radius-one local and hence radius-\(r\) local because \(r\ge1\).  The outcome envelope follows from \(|V_{i,c}|=b\le B\).  Moreover
\(\pi_i(e_1)=\pi_i(e_0)=1/2\ge\varepsilon\), since the declared overlap constant satisfies \(\varepsilon<1/2\).  Together with the iid innovations and the two conditionally independent Bernoulli waves, these facts verify every condition defining \(P_t\in\mathcal M_{2,\mathrm{loc}}\).

For a realized schedule \(V_i=v\), direct averaging over the four equiprobable local assignment cells gives
\[
 m_i
 =\mathbb E_{P_t}\!\left[
 Y_i(D^{(w)};U,G)
 \left\{\frac{\mathbf 1(D_i^{(w)}=1)}{1/2}
 -\frac{\mathbf 1(D_i^{(w)}=0)}{1/2}\right\}
 \middle|\mathcal F_U\right]
 =\frac{v_{10}+v_{11}-v_{00}-v_{01}}2. \tag{4}
\]
Thus \(m_i=0\) on \(\mathcal H_0\), whereas (4) equals \(a\) at \(v^+\) and \(-a\) at \(v^-\).  The symmetry of \(Q_t\) gives \(\tau_{\mathrm P}=\mathbb E_{P_t}m_i=0\).  Since the schedules are iid across sites, \((h_i)=(m_i)\) is iid, and hence
\[
 \gamma_h(0)=\mathbb E_{P_t}m_i^2=a^2t,
 \qquad
 \gamma_h(k)=0\quad(k\ne0),
 \qquad
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}(P_t)=a^2t. \tag{5}
\]
In particular, \(P_0\) is a null law and every \(P_t\), \(t>0\), is a positive alternative.  Equation (4) also proves that the parameter moved in (5) is the causal conditional exposure-effect score, rather than an arbitrary observed-law functional.

It remains to bound the information in the complete observation.  Condition on both assignment arrays.  At site \(i\), the two observed outcomes select the ordered cell pair \((c,c')=(C_i(D^{(1)}),C_i(D^{(2)}))\).  Write \(R_j^{c,c'}\) for the law of \((V_{i,c},V_{i,c'})\) under \(Q_j\), \(j\in\{0,1\}\), and list atom probabilities in the order \((b,b),(b,-b),(-b,b),(-b,-b)\).  Exhaustive enumeration of the six schedules in \(\mathcal H_0\) and the two schedules \(v^+,v^-\) gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
\text{ordered cell pair}&R_0^{c,c'}&R_1^{c,c'}\\ \hline
c=c'&(1/2,0,0,1/2)&(1/2,0,0,1/2)\\
c\ne c'\text{ within }\{00,01\}\text{ or }\{10,11\}
 &(1/6,1/3,1/3,1/6)&(1/2,0,0,1/2)\\
c\text{ and }c'\text{ in opposite exposure groups}
 &(1/3,1/6,1/6,1/3)&(0,1/2,1/2,0).
\end{array} \tag{6}
\]
The three rows cover all sixteen ordered pairs in \(\mathcal C^2\), so (6) is also the exact smallest-cell stress test.  In every row, each atom charged by \(R_1^{c,c'}\) has positive \(R_0^{c,c'}\)-probability.  Therefore the two-wave raw outcome law has common support even though the latent four-cell schedule law in (2) does not.

Let \(R_t^{c,c'}=(1-t)R_0^{c,c'}+tR_1^{c,c'}\).  For distinct cells, direct substitution from (6) yields
\[
 \sum_x\frac{\{R_1^{c,c'}(x)-R_0^{c,c'}(x)\}^2}{R_0^{c,c'}(x)}=2, \tag{7}
\]
while the same quantity is zero when \(c=c'\).  Since \(\log u\le u-1\) for \(u>0\),
\[
 \operatorname{KL}(R_t^{c,c'}\Vert R_0^{c,c'})
 \le \sum_x\frac{\{R_t^{c,c'}(x)-R_0^{c,c'}(x)\}^2}{R_0^{c,c'}(x)}
 \le2t^2. \tag{8}
\]
Conditional on the assignments, the selected outcome pairs are independent over \(i\in I_n\), because the schedules \(V_i\) are independent.  The graph is the same deterministic line under \(P_t\) and \(P_0\); the assignments have the same law; and the exposures and propensity coordinates are deterministic functions of the graph and assignments.  Expanding the conditional product likelihood ratio, taking its logarithm, and then averaging first over the independent schedules and then over the common assignment law proves
\[
 \operatorname{KL}\!\left(\mathcal L_{P_t}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})
 \middle\Vert\mathcal L_{P_0}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\right)
 =\mathbb E_D\sum_{i\in I_n}
 \operatorname{KL}(R_t^{C_i(D^{(1)}),C_i(D^{(2)})}\Vert
 R_0^{C_i(D^{(1)}),C_i(D^{(2)})})
 \le2N_nt^2. \tag{9}
\]
Thus (9) is a chain-rule likelihood bound for the entire declared observation, not merely for its score coordinates.

Put \(\eta=1-\alpha-\beta>0\) and
\[
 t_0=\frac{\eta}{\sqrt{2N_n}}.
\]
Because \(0<\eta<1\) and \(N_n\ge1\), one has \(0<t_0<1\).  Pinsker's inequality and (9) give
\[
 \operatorname{TV}\!\left(\mathcal L_{P_{t_0}}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}}),
 \mathcal L_{P_0}(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\right)
 \le\sqrt{N_nt_0^2}=\frac{\eta}{\sqrt2}. \tag{10}
\]
Let \(\varphi_n\in\Phi_n^{\mathrm{obs}}\) be any randomized test satisfying
\(\mathbb E_{P_0}\varphi_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\le\alpha\).  To use the binary form of the two-point testing lemma, adjoin under both laws a common independent \(A\sim\operatorname{Uniform}[0,1]\) and reject when \(A\le\varphi_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})\).  Integrating measurable sections shows that taking the product with this same uniform law leaves total variation unchanged.  The two-point lemma and (10) then imply
\[
 \mathbb E_{P_{t_0}}[1-\varphi_n(O_n^{\mathrm{obs}})]
 \ge1-\alpha-\frac{\eta}{\sqrt2}
 =\beta+\eta\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)>\beta. \tag{11}
\]
By (5),
\[
 \Omega_{\mathrm{pop}}(P_{t_0})
 =\frac{a^2(1-\alpha-\beta)}{\sqrt{2N_n}}. \tag{12}
\]
For every candidate separation no larger than (12), the law \(P_{t_0}\) is in the corresponding alternative set and violates the required type-II bound in (11).  Taking the infimum in the definition of \(s_{n,\alpha,\beta}^{\mathrm{obs}}\) proves the lower bound.  Combining it with (1), choosing any fixed positive \(a\le2B\), using \(N_n=n-2r\), and using the established \(\rho_n(\alpha,\beta)=O(n^{-1/2})\) proves the asserted \(\Theta(n^{-1/2})\) rate.  The condition \(e_1\ne e_0\) is necessary: if the two labels coincide, the two terms in every exposure-IPW score cancel identically.
body.justification: This theorem certifies root-sample-size optimality even when a test uses the complete declared experimental record rather than only precomputed scores.
body.gap: Viviano2020 studies pilot-based second-wave design optimization, not a common-support information lower bound for testing the Palm covariance boundary.
body.consumer: A designer can use the finite-sample upper threshold knowing that no common Borel test of the declared full observation improves its separation order uniformly over the class.
